vignette:
The night of the fire, Marcus was on the phone with his younger brother, Leo. He heard the crash first, then the shouting, then the wet, percussive sound of a body hitting the floor. He listened, frozen, as Leo's girlfriend screamed and the sirens began to wail. He could not move from his couch; he could only hear his brother's breathing stop. That was eighteen months ago. Leo survived, but Marcus has not. The memory lives in him not as a story he can tell, but as a series of snapshots-photographic, still, and silent-that slide into his mind without warning. When he tries to explain what happened, the words fail him; the event exists only in images and in the acrid, metallic smell of smoke and blood that sometimes fills his nostrils for no reason he can identify. He has come to believe that his own body is betraying him, that these reactions mean he is still in danger, even when he knows, logically, that the fire is long over. Because he is now certain that danger is everywhere and that his own instincts cannot be trusted, ordinary moments become mined with threat - a stranger's sudden laugh, a car door slamming, a neighbor's raised voice all feel like the beginning of another catastrophe.

Marcus is twenty-one, married, and unemployed. He used to work as a stock clerk in a grocery warehouse, but he stopped going after a co-worker made a passing comment about how dangerous family life could be. That single remark sent him home shaking, and he never returned. Now, any comment about family-whether on television, in a song, or overheard in a café-feels like a threat directed at him. He has become hypervigilant to the way people move. A sudden gesture from his wife, a stranger reaching into a pocket, a car braking too quickly-each one puts him immediately on guard. He cannot sleep. Most nights he lies awake, replaying the images, waiting for something else to happen. He is certain that if he lets his guard down, something terrible will strike again, and he will not be able to protect anyone.

Because he cannot trust his own vigilance, he has developed a set of rules to keep himself safe. He avoids all media that might depict violence or accidents-no crime shows, no news, no movies with sirens. He cannot bear to be alone in the apartment, so his wife has rearranged her work schedule to be home more often, a change that has strained their finances and their marriage. When the pressure inside him becomes unbearable, he cuts his forearms with a razor blade; the physical pain, he says, is the only thing that stops the images from cycling. But the self-harm also brings the memory back more vividly-the smell of smoke always returns afterward, and the photographic images flash more intensely for hours. He has found that the more he avoids, the more the memories intrude, and the more he feels he cannot rely on himself to cope.

His wife has started to notice that he flinches when she walks into a room too quickly. He knows this hurts her, but he cannot stop it. The threat he perceives in sudden movements is immediate and overwhelming, and it drives him deeper into avoidance. He has begun to believe that he is no longer capable of the things that used to define him-being a reliable partner, a protective older brother, a steady worker. He sees himself as broken, and that belief makes him scan the world even more anxiously for signs of danger. A person acting suspiciously on the street, a comment about family from a stranger, a glimpse of a burned hand or a scarred arm-each trigger confirms his appraisal that the world is unsafe and he is unequal to it. He has not visited Leo in the hospital since the first week. He cannot bear to see his brother's scars. The sight of those specific body parts-the mottled skin on Leo's forearm-would send him into a flashback so vivid he might believe he is back in that moment, listening to the phone line go dead.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a night last week when his wife found him standing in the bathroom, razor in hand, unable to speak. She told him she was afraid to leave him alone. He realized then that his fear of being alone had created the very thing he feared most: he could not be trusted by the person he loved. He is terrified that the memories will never stop, that he will never feel safe again, and that his marriage will not survive his silence. But he is also desperate enough to try anything. He wants to know if there is a way to put the fire out.
